key_terms.meaning: An analytical device that pairs a biological recognition element with a transducer to give a measurable signal that rises with one analyte
The biological part (enzyme, antibody, nucleic acid, cell, receptor) that binds or reacts with only the target analyte
The physical part that converts the biological event into an electrical signal: current, voltage, light or mass change
Plot of signal (y) against known standard concentrations (x); slope = sensitivity, intercept = background
Lowest concentration that can be told apart from the blank; LOD = 3σ/S, with σ the standard deviation of the blank and S the calibration slope
Ability to respond to the target while ignoring similar molecules such as other sugars or other proteins
Substrate concentration at which the enzyme rate is half of V<sub>max</sub>; the response is nearly straight only well below K<sub>m</sub>
Measurement of current at a fixed electrode potential; current is proportional to the concentration of electroactive species
Measurement of voltage at near-zero current; voltage follows the Nernst equation, about 59 mV per decade at 25 °C
Fixing the enzyme or antibody onto the electrode surface by adsorption, covalent bonding, cross-linking or entrapment
Ion-sensitive field-effect transistor: a MOSFET whose metal gate is replaced by ion-selective membrane plus sample, so surface charge shifts threshold voltage
Gate voltage at which the MOSFET channel just forms; in an ISFET it moves with the charge on the membrane surface
Immunologically sensitive FET: antibody layer on the gate; antigen binding changes charge and shifts V<sub>T</sub>
Needle enzyme electrode left in interstitial fluid for days, giving a reading every few minutes, with a lag of roughly 5–15 minutes behind blood
Pairing of a single-stranded probe with its complementary target strand to form a double helix
One-molecule-thick ordered film, typically an alkanethiol on gold, used to attach probes and block bare surface
Hairpin DNA with a redox tag at one end; hybridisation opens the stem, moves the tag away from the electrode and lowers the current
Distance over which a surface charge is screened by ions in solution; about 0.7–0.8 nm in 150 mM salt
Semiconductor nanocrystal (for example CdSe) whose emission colour is set by particle size, used as an optical or electrochemical label
Size- and shape-dependent light absorption of metal nanoparticles that shifts when molecules bind to their surface
Förster resonance energy transfer: non-radiative energy transfer from a donor to a nearby acceptor, E = 1/(1 + (r/R<sub>0</sub>)<sup>6</sup>)
Antigen concentration at which half the antibody sites are filled; θ = [Ag]/(K<sub>d</sub> + [Ag]); smaller K<sub>d</sub> means tighter binding

takeaways: A biosensor is only a system: recognition element, transducer and electronics, and no reading is trusted until it is calibrated against standards.
Selectivity comes from the biological element; the usable range and detection limit come from its binding or catalytic kinetics.
Electrochemical transducers are popular because they are cheap, small and give a direct electrical signal that a simple circuit can digitise.

In an ISFET the sample and a reference electrode take the place of the metal gate, so the measured quantity is a shift in threshold voltage: about 59 mV per pH at 25 °C, read at constant drain current.
The disposable glucose strip is the most widely used biosensor in the world, and the continuous monitor turns the same chemistry into a time trace.
DNA biosensors trade the enzyme's amplification for sequence specificity, and read the amount of duplex formed by current or impedance.
At the nanoscale, high surface area amplifies small binding events, but charge screening by salt limits what can be detected electrically.
Every number on a biosensor report comes from calibration: sensitivity is the slope, the detection limit is 3σ/S, and standard addition corrects for the sample matrix.
bank_note: Long answers here usually begin with the recognition-element–transducer pair, then move to calibration, limit of detection and controls, and finish with one worked device such as the glucose strip, the ISFET or the DNA electrode.

bank.q: Define a biosensor. Name its three essential components and state the function of each, with one medical and one environmental example.
outline: Definition linking biological recognition to a measurable signal proportional to one analyte
Bio-recognition element: enzyme, antibody, nucleic acid, cell or receptor
Transducer: electrochemical, optical, piezoelectric or thermal
Electronics: amplification, digitisation, display
Example: glucose strip (medical); pesticide or BOD sensor (environment)
answer: Definition. A biosensor is an analytical device in which a biological recognition element is held in close contact with a transducer, so that the recognition event becomes an electrical signal that rises with the concentration of one analyte.

head: Component
Function
Glucose-strip example
rows: binds or reacts with the analyte only; gives selectivity
turns the reaction into current, voltage, light, mass or heat
carbon electrode at a fixed potential
amplify, filter, digitise, convert with the calibration, display

answer: Recognition element. An enzyme catalyses one reaction (glucose oxidase on glucose), an antibody binds one antigen, a DNA probe pairs with one sequence, and whole cells respond to toxins. This layer decides what is measured.

Transducer. Amperometric (current at fixed potential), potentiometric (voltage at zero current), optical, piezoelectric or calorimetric. It must touch the recognition layer, or the product diffuses away before it is sensed.

Electronics. For an amperometric strip, Faraday's law gives I = nFJA. With n = 2, J = 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol cm⁻² s⁻¹ and A = 0.020 cm², I = 2 × 96 485 × 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.020 = 1.93 µA. A transimpedance amplifier with Rf = 100 kΩ turns this into 0.193 V, which the ADC digitises and the stored calibration converts to mmol/L.
Medical example. The disposable glucose strip: glucose oxidase and a mediator on a printed carbon electrode, read in about 5 s from a finger-prick drop.

Environmental example. A biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) sensor: immobilised microbes over an oxygen electrode; organic matter in the water makes the microbes breathe faster, so the oxygen current falls. An acetylcholinesterase electrode for pesticides works the other way: the pesticide inhibits the enzyme and the signal drops.
Calibration. No reading is trusted until the device has been calibrated against standards and checked with a blank and controls.

Why calibration and controls matter. The same strip chemistry can drift with storage temperature and age. A lot calibration code, a control solution of known glucose and a check that the reading falls inside the control range are what make the displayed number trustworthy.
Check. 1.93 µA × 100 kΩ = 0.193 V, well inside a 3 V supply, so the chain can carry a fivefold higher glucose without saturating.

bank.q: Explain how a biosensor differs from an ordinary chemical or physical sensor, and why the biological element is the source of selectivity.
outline: Physical sensor responds to a bulk property; chemical sensor responds to a class of species
Biological element gives molecular recognition through shape and charge complementarity
Enzyme active site, antigen–antibody fit, base pairing
Selectivity measured against interfering species
Selectivity does not fix range or LOD; kinetics do
answer: Physical sensor. Responds to a bulk physical quantity: a thermistor to temperature, a strain gauge to force. It has no chemical selectivity at all.

Chemical sensor. Responds to a class of chemical species through a non-biological layer: a glass electrode to H⁺, a valinomycin membrane to K⁺, a metal-oxide film to reducing gases. Its selectivity comes from the glass, the membrane or the oxide.

Biosensor. Adds a biological recognition element. A glass electrode cannot tell glucose from fructose, because neither changes H⁺ directly; glucose oxidase over an electrode can, because only glucose fits its active site well.

Why the biological element gives selectivity. Biological molecules recognise shape and charge together. (1) The enzyme active site holds the substrate by several weak bonds at fixed positions, so a sugar with one hydroxyl group in the wrong place binds poorly. (2) An antibody's binding pocket matches the shape and charge of one epitope, with Kd often in the nanomolar range. (3) A DNA probe pairs base by base, A with T and G with C, so one wrong base lowers Tm by about 5 °C.

Reading the table. The enzyme rejects galactose fiftyfold (100/2 = 50). Ascorbic acid is not a substrate at all, but it is oxidised directly at the electrode; this is a transducer problem, solved by a mediator at a lower potential or a blocking membrane, not by the enzyme.

Selectivity is not range. The enzyme sets which molecule is measured; its kinetics set how much. With Km = 25 mmol/L the response at 20 mmol/L is only 25/45 = 0.56 of the straight-line value. A selective sensor can still have a poor range or a high detection limit.
Price of the biological element. Biomolecules denature with heat, pH and time, so biosensors have shelf lives and need cold storage and lot calibration, which a glass electrode does not.

Numbers on the chemical side. A glass electrode follows 59.16 mV per pH at 25 °C for any source of H⁺. Lactic acid, carbon dioxide and a buffer change all move it the same way, so it reports acidity, never the molecule that caused it.

bank.q: Classify biosensors by bio-recognition element and by transducer type, giving one example of each class.
outline: By recognition: enzyme, antibody, DNA, cell, microbial, aptamer
By transducer: amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric, optical, piezoelectric, calorimetric
Calorimetric and piezoelectric explained in one line each
Example device for each class
Note that a single analyte can be measured by more than one class
answer: Two independent axes. A biosensor is named by what recognises the analyte and by what turns recognition into a signal; any recognition element can in principle sit on any transducer.

head: Class
What it does
Example
rows: DNA electrode for a pathogen gene
folded synthetic DNA or RNA that binds a target
cell metabolism responds to the analyte

head: Class
Held / measured
Example
rows: zero current / voltage, 59.16 mV per decade at 25 °C
mass on a quartz crystal / resonant frequency

answer: Piezoelectric in one line. A quartz crystal oscillates at a fixed frequency, and mass bound to its surface lowers that frequency in proportion.
Calorimetric in one line. Most enzyme reactions release heat, and a thermistor in the enzyme column reads the small temperature rise, which is proportional to the amount converted.
Generations of enzyme sensors. First generation uses oxygen as the electron acceptor; second uses a mediator such as ferricyanide; third transfers electrons directly from enzyme to electrode.

One analyte, several classes. Urea can be read by urease with a potentiometric ammonium electrode (a change of 40 mV is 40/59.16 = 0.68 decade, a 4.75-fold change in urea), with an EnFET, or with a conductometric cell; glucose by amperometry, by an optical oxygen sensor or by a thermistor.

Choosing. Electrochemical classes dominate cheap disposable tests because they need only a few electrodes and a simple circuit; optical and piezoelectric classes suit label-free laboratory binding studies.

Label-free against labelled. A second cut, used for antibody and DNA sensors, is whether binding is seen directly (impedance, FET, SPR, quartz mass) or through a label (enzyme, fluorophore, redox tag, gold particle). Labels raise the signal but add steps.
Check. Every row pairs one element and one transducer, so the two tables together cover the whole classification.

bank.q: Explain Michaelis–Menten kinetics and show how Km and Vmax set the useful measuring range of an enzyme electrode.
outline: Rate equation and meaning of Vmax and Km
First-order region at low substrate, zero-order at high substrate
Linear range sits where signal is proportional to concentration
Immobilisation lowers activity and can shift apparent Km
Diffusion limitation in a thick film widens or narrows the range
Link to detection limit and saturation point
answer: Rate equation. v = Vmax S / (Km + S). Vmax is the rate with every active site busy; Km is the substrate concentration at which v = Vmax/2.
Origin in one line. Enzyme and substrate form a complex that either falls apart or turns into product; at steady state the fraction of enzyme in the complex is S/(Km + S).
Two limits. For S ≪ Km, v ≈ (Vmax/Km) S: first order, straight in S, the useful measuring region. For S ≫ Km, v ≈ Vmax: zero order, the signal no longer changes with S.

Setting the range. The ratio of actual to straight-line response is Km/(Km + S). If a 10 % departure from a straight line is allowed, the range ends at S = Km/9: 2.8 mmol/L for Km = 25 and 6.7 mmol/L for Km = 60. Beyond that a curved calibration is needed, and above about 19 Km nothing can be resolved.

Immobilisation. Fixing the enzyme lowers its activity (fewer accessible sites, wrong orientation) and, because substrate must diffuse through the layer, raises the apparent Km. A deliberate diffusion-limiting membrane goes further: the electrode then responds to the substrate flux through the membrane, which is proportional to S over a wide range. This is how glucose strips reach about 30 mmol/L with an enzyme whose solution Km is lower.
Detection limit. The lower end is set by noise: LOD = 3σ/Scal, with Scal the initial slope. A larger Vmax/Km, more enzyme or a larger electrode, raises the slope and lowers the LOD.
Trade-off. A higher apparent Km widens the linear range but lowers the slope (Vmax/Km = 120/60 = 2.0 instead of 120/25 = 4.8), so the LOD rises by 4.8/2.0 = 2.4 times.
Check. At S = Km both columns give exactly Vmax/2 at their own Km: 120 × 25/50 = 60 and 120 × 60/120 = 60.

bank.q: Describe the structure and principle of an ISFET, and explain how it differs from a MOSFET.
outline: MOSFET structure: source, drain, gate oxide, metal gate
ISFET: metal gate replaced by ion-selective membrane, sample and reference electrode
Surface charge at the sensing layer shifts the threshold voltage
Nernstian response, about 59 mV per pH unit at 25 °C
Difference: input is ionic activity in solution, not a gate voltage
Drift and reference electrode issues
answer: MOSFET. n⁺ source and drain in p-silicon, a thin SiO₂ gate oxide, and a metal gate. A gate voltage above the threshold VT forms an n-channel and drain current ID flows.

ISFET. The metal gate is removed. A sensing layer of Si₃N₄ or Ta₂O₅ is deposited on the gate oxide, the sample electrolyte covers it, and a Ag/AgCl reference electrode in the sample sets the gate voltage. Everything except the gate window is sealed with epoxy or polyimide.

head: Feature
MOSFET
ISFET
rows: reference electrode, electrolyte, sensing layer on oxide

answer: Principle. H⁺ ions bind to SiOH or TaOH sites on the sensing layer. The bound charge changes the surface potential, which adds in series with the applied gate voltage and so shifts the effective VT. The ideal shift is the Nernst slope, 2.303RT/F = 59.16 mV per pH at 25 °C.

Readout. At constant drain current, a feedback loop moves VG to cancel the shift, so VG follows pH: a fall from 7.4 to 7.1 moves VG by 59.16 × 0.3 = 17.7 mV. At constant VG in the subthreshold region with a swing of 70 mV per decade, ID changes by 1017.7/70 = 1.79 times.
Variants. An enzyme layer makes an EnFET (urease, penicillinase, glucose oxidase); an antibody layer makes an IMFET, limited by Debye screening to binding within about 1 nm in serum.

Practical problems. Drift as the layer hydrates, hysteresis, light sensitivity of the silicon, temperature (61.55 mV per pH at 37 °C) and above all the reference electrode, whose drift adds straight to VG. A differential pair with a reference FET cancels common drift.
Advantages over a glass electrode. Small, robust, batch-made on a wafer, fast, and low output impedance, so it suits catheters and arrays.

Fabrication in one line. The ISFET is made with ordinary CMOS steps: field oxide, source and drain diffusion, thin gate oxide, sensing-layer deposition, contacts, then encapsulation that leaves only the gate window open.

bank.q: A glucose sensor gives readings of 12, 26, 51, 98 and 190 nA for standards of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 mmol/L. Find the sensitivity and, if the blank gives 3.0 ± 0.6 nA, the limit of detection.
outline: Plot or fit signal against concentration; slope in nA per mmol/L
Sensitivity from slope, check linearity and intercept
Blank signal plus 3 × standard deviation of blank
Convert that signal to concentration using the slope
State LOD with units
Comment on whether the standard addition method is needed for a real sample matrix
answer: Data. Standards x = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 mmol/L give y = 12, 26, 51, 98, 190 nA. Blank 3.0 ± 0.6 nA.
Sensitivity. Slope = Sxy/Sxx = 1754.6/148.8 = 11.79 nA per mmol/L.
Intercept. b = ȳ − slope × x̄ = 75.4 − 11.79 × 6.2 = 75.4 − 73.1 = 2.3 nA, close to the measured blank of 3.0 nA, as it should be.

Linearity check. Predicted values 14.1, 25.9, 49.5, 96.6 and 191.0 nA differ from the readings by −2.1, +0.1, +1.5, +1.4 and −1.0 nA, all under 2.1 nA, and r² = 0.9995. The line is straight up to 16 mmol/L. As a rough check, the end points give (190 − 12)/(16 − 1) = 11.9 nA per mmol/L.
Limit of detection. LOD = 3σ/S = 3 × 0.6 / 11.79 = 0.15 mmol/L.

Same result as a signal. The decision signal is blank + 3σ = 3.0 + 1.8 = 4.8 nA. Read on the line, (4.8 − 2.3)/11.79 = 0.21 mmol/L; the two routes differ because the fitted intercept (2.3 nA) is not exactly the measured blank (3.0 nA). Report the method used.

Real samples. Standards were in clean buffer. Serum or whole blood can lower the slope through viscosity, protein fouling and interferents, so a standard addition on the sample (spike, re-read, correct for the added volume) shows whether the slope in the matrix is still 11.79 nA per mmol/L.

Reporting. State the result as sensitivity 11.8 nA per mmol/L, linear from 1 to 16 mmol/L (r² = 0.9995), LOD 0.15 mmol/L by 3σ/S with σ = 0.6 nA from blank readings. Name the blank and the number of repeats used to find σ.
Check. 11.79 × 8 + 2.3 = 96.6 nA against the measured 98 nA.

bank.q: Design a disposable amperometric glucose sensor strip for a home meter. Choose the enzyme, the immobilisation method, the electrode material, the applied potential and the calibration scheme, and justify each choice.
outline: Glucose oxidase or dehydrogenase; reaction producing H₂O₂ or using a mediator
Immobilisation by cross-linking or entrapment in a printed film
Screen-printed carbon working electrode, Ag/AgCl reference
Potential about 0.6–0.7 V for H₂O₂, or lower with a mediator
Nafion or similar membrane to cut interference from uric acid and ascorbate
Two-point calibration per strip batch, coding, fingerstick confirmatory tests
answer: Requirements. A cheap, dry, single-use strip that reads 1–30 mmol/L from about 1 µL of capillary blood in about 5 s, independent of blood oxygen, with a stable lot calibration.

Enzyme. Glucose oxidase (GOx): very selective for β-D-glucose, cheap and robust. Glucose dehydrogenase with a FAD cofactor is the alternative when oxygen independence matters most; it avoids oxygen entirely but must be chosen so maltose and xylose do not react.

Electron route. Ferricyanide mediator, not oxygen: reduced GOx passes electrons to Fe(CN)₆³⁻, and the electrode reoxidises Fe(CN)₆⁴⁻. This removes the oxygen dependence of the first-generation H₂O₂ route.

Applied potential. About +0.3 to +0.4 V against Ag/AgCl for the mediator, instead of +0.6 to +0.7 V for H₂O₂. Ascorbic and uric acid still oxidise partly at this potential, so a Nafion layer or a blank electrode is added.

Electrodes and immobilisation. Screen-printed carbon working electrode, Ag/AgCl reference, and a fill-detect pair at the far end of the capillary. GOx and mediator are dried in a hydrophilic polymer film over the working electrode; cross-linking with glutaraldehyde or entrapment keeps them in place.

head: Quantity
Choice
Result
rows: about 0.97 V, inside a 3 V supply

answer: Calibration scheme. Each manufacturing lot is calibrated against a laboratory plasma method, and the slope and intercept are stored as a code or chip read by the meter, so the user does no calibration. The meter reports plasma-equivalent glucose and corrects for temperature with an on-board thermistor. Control solutions at two levels check meter and strips.

Error control. Fill detection stops short-sample errors; a second, enzyme-free electrode measures the interferent current for subtraction; haematocrit is estimated from an AC impedance reading and corrected.

Packaging and storage. Strips are sealed in a vial with a desiccant, because moisture slowly reduces the dried mediator and raises the blank; the vial carries an expiry date, and the meter refuses strips whose blank current is too high.
Check. 1.93 µA × 5 × 100 kΩ = 0.965 V, so the full range fits the supply.

bank.q: An ISFET with a Nernstian slope of 59 mV per pH unit is used for a urea sensor. Calculate the threshold shift for a pH change of 0.05 and explain two reasons a measured shift may not match this figure.
outline: Sign follows direction of pH change
Reason 1: membrane drift and hydration over hours
Reason 2: reference electrode instability or junction potential
Reason 3: incomplete urease conversion at low urea or short residence time
Calibration and blank correction before any reading is quoted
answer: Principle. Urease hydrolyses urea: CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O → 2NH₃ + CO₂. Ammonia takes up H⁺, so the local pH at the gate rises, and the pH ISFET under the enzyme layer reads that rise.
Threshold shift. ΔV = 59 mV per pH × 0.05 pH = 2.95 mV.

Sign. The pH rises, so H⁺ leaves the surface sites, the surface potential falls and, at constant drain current, the feedback gate voltage moves in the opposite direction to the shift for a pH fall: if a fall of 0.3 pH moved VG down by 17.7 mV, a rise of 0.05 moves it up by 2.95 mV.

Reason 1: drift. The sensing layer hydrates over hours and VT creeps, often by tenths of a millivolt to a few millivolts per hour. Against a 2.95 mV signal that is a large error unless a reference FET without urease subtracts it.
Reason 2: reference electrode. The Ag/AgCl potential and its liquid junction drift with chloride and temperature; any change adds directly to VG.

Reason 3: buffer and enzyme. The sample buffer soaks up part of the ammonia, so the pH change depends on buffer capacity as much as on urea; and at low urea or a short contact time the urease conversion is incomplete. The slope of an EnFET is therefore set by calibration with urea standards, not by the Nernst value.
Reason 4: sub-Nernstian surface. Si₃N₄ often gives 45–56 mV per pH rather than 59, so the measured shift would be 2.3–2.8 mV.
Practice. Calibrate the EnFET with two or three urea standards in the same buffer, run a reference FET, control temperature, and quote readings only after the blank has been subtracted.

Two-point calibration. If 5 and 20 mmol/L urea standards give 2.4 and 6.0 mV, the working slope is (6.0 − 2.4)/15 = 0.24 mV per mmol/L over that range; samples are read from this line, not from the Nernst value.

Worked contrast. A pH fall of 0.30 at constant drain current moved VG by 17.7 mV; the urea signal here is six times smaller, which is why an EnFET is always read differentially against a reference FET without enzyme.

bank.q: Design a DNA biosensor to detect a known single-base mutation. Describe the probe, its attachment, the hybridisation step, the signal readout, the controls and the stringency wash.
outline: Short probe matched to the mutant sequence, 15–30 bases
Thiol probe on gold through a self-assembled monolayer, backfilled to control spacing
Hybridisation in buffer at chosen salt and temperature
Readout: redox label, intercalator current, or impedance change
Positive control target, negative control mismatched target, blank
Stringency wash: raised temperature or lowered salt melts mismatched duplex
Single-base discrimination demonstrated by comparing signals
answer: Goal. Tell a sample with a known single-base mutation from the normal (wild-type) sequence.

Probe. A 20-base synthetic strand complementary to the mutant sequence, with the mutation near the middle, where one mismatch destabilises the duplex most. Example: A = 5, T = 5, G = 5, C = 5 gives Tm = 2(10) + 4(10) = 60 °C by the Wallace rule. A T10 linker and a 5' thiol are added.

Attachment. Clean gold electrode in 0.1–1 µM thiolated probe for 1–16 h; Au–S bonds form a self-assembled monolayer. Backfill with 1 mM 6-mercapto-1-hexanol for about 1 h so the probes stand up and bare gold is blocked.
Sample preparation. Amplify the region by PCR or an isothermal method, heat to 95 °C for 5 min to separate the strands, and cool fast on ice.
Hybridisation. Apply the single strands in buffer with enough Na⁺ to shield the backbones, at 55 °C (Tm − 5) for this probe.

Stringency wash. Same temperature and salt, or slightly hotter or lower in salt. The mutant target forms a perfect duplex (Tm 60 °C) and stays; the wild-type target has one mismatch (Tm about 55 °C), so about half of it has separated at 55 °C and is washed away; a slightly hotter wash removes more.
Alternative readouts. Methylene blue intercalator current after the wash, a ferrocene-tagged signalling probe, or an E-DNA stem-loop whose current falls on binding.

Controls. A blank electrode, a positive control (synthetic mutant target), a negative control (synthetic wild-type target) on the same chip, and a calibrated decision threshold between them, for example 75 %.
Decision. A sample giving 150 % is mutant; 30 % is wild type; a value near 90 % suggests a heterozygous sample with both strands and is repeated.

Why the mutation sits in the middle. A mismatch at the end of the probe leaves most of the duplex intact and changes Tm by only 1–2 °C; in the middle it splits the duplex into two short halves and lowers Tm by about 5 °C, which the wash can use.
Check. Match-to-mismatch ratio = 150/30 = 5.0, enough to separate the two with a single threshold.

bank.q: A home test uses gold nanoparticles with an antibody sandwich for a cardiac marker. Explain how the LSPR signal arises, why nanoparticles amplify small binding events, and what limits the test.
outline: LSPR absorption depends on particle size, shape and spacing
Binding of antigen and second antibody layer changes local refractive index
Shift in wavelength or colour change read by eye or simple optics
Optical readout avoids charge screening by salt
Limits: antibody cross-reactivity, matrix effects in whole blood, batch-to-batch particle size, quantitation accuracy
answer: Format. A lateral-flow strip: sample pad, conjugate pad with gold nanoparticles carrying antibody 1, a nitrocellulose membrane with a test line of antibody 2 and a control line of anti-species antibody, and an absorbent pad that pulls the liquid along.

How LSPR arises. Light drives the conduction electrons of a 20–40 nm gold particle to oscillate together. At about 520 nm this oscillation resonates, so the particle absorbs and scatters green light strongly and looks red. The peak depends on size, shape and spacing: aggregated particles couple and shift the absorption to longer wavelengths, so the colour moves to blue-purple.

Signal at the line. The cardiac marker (for example troponin) is sandwiched between gold–antibody 1 and the fixed antibody 2, so gold piles up at the test line and the line turns red. The control line captures excess conjugate whatever the sample, showing the strip has run.

Why nanoparticles amplify. Each bound antigen brings a whole particle whose extinction is enormous for its size: one 40 nm gold particle absorbs about as strongly as many thousands of dye molecules. A modest number of binding events therefore gives a line visible by eye, with no instrument.
Optical advantage. The readout is colour, not charge, so it is not limited by Debye screening (about 0.8 nm in serum); the antigen can bind anywhere on the antibody.

Binding limit (illustrative numbers). Troponin I has a mass of about 24 kDa. A level of 50 ng/L is 50 × 10⁻⁹ / 24 000 = 2.1 × 10⁻¹² mol/L. With an assumed Kd of 0.1 nmol/L, the fraction of capture sites filled is θ = 2.1 × 10⁻¹² / (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ + 2.1 × 10⁻¹²) = 0.020, about 2 %. That is why home cardiac tests are qualitative and only detect clearly raised levels.

Limits. Cross-reactivity of the antibodies; whole-blood matrix (red cells filtered out by the pad, viscosity changing the flow); batch-to-batch particle size changing the colour; the high-dose hook effect, where a very high antigen level saturates both antibodies separately and the line fades; and poor quantitation by eye. A small reader that measures line intensity improves the last point.
Clinical caution. A negative home test does not rule out a heart attack; chest pain still needs hospital assessment.

bank.q: A continuous glucose monitor reads 4.2 mmol/L while the fingerstick reads 6.0 mmol/L on day 6 of wear, with the gap widening after meals. Analyse the likely causes and state how calibration and alarms should be handled.
outline: Interstitial fluid lag behind blood, exaggerated by rising or falling glucose
Sensor drift and enzyme decay over wear time
Pressure-induced changes in local perfusion at night
Calibration: fingerstick calibration points, time limits on calibration validity
Trend arrows rather than single points; alarms set on rate of change
Accuracy expressed as mean absolute relative difference against reference
Rule that a reading is confirmed with a fingerstick before dosing
answer: The gap. Sensor 4.2 against finger-stick 6.0 mmol/L: an absolute difference of 1.8 mmol/L, and a relative difference of 1.8/6.0 = 30 %, about three times a typical MARD of under 10 %.

Cause 1: physiological lag. The sensor reads interstitial fluid, which follows blood by about 5–15 min. After a meal glucose rises; if it rises at 0.15 mmol/L per minute, a 12 min lag alone puts the sensor 0.15 × 12 = 1.8 mmol/L low. This fits the gap that widens after meals.

Cause 2: sensor ageing. On day 6 the enzyme has partly lost activity and the membrane has fouled with protein, so the sensitivity has fallen. If the sensitivity has dropped by 10 %, a true 6.0 reads 5.4 even without lag.

Cause 3: local effects. Pressure on the sensor (a compression low, mostly at night) cuts local blood flow; inflammation around the wire consumes glucose. These give falsely low readings independent of meals.

Calibration. Calibrate only when the trend arrow is flat (glucose changing under about 0.05 mmol/L per minute), never right after a meal or insulin. A calibration taken at this moment would wrongly raise the sensor gain by 6.0/4.2 = 1.43 and then over-read for hours. If the steady-state gap stays above about 20 %, replace the sensor.

Alarms. The sensor is near the low alarm (3.9 mmol/L) while blood is normal, so false low alarms will follow. Use rate-of-change and predictive alarms, and confirm any low or any dosing decision with a finger-stick.
Accuracy reporting. MARD over paired readings; for example 9.09, 7.14, 11.11 and 5.00 % average to 8.1 %. Accuracy is worst in the low range, where a fixed error is a larger share.
Conclusion. The widening gap after meals points to lag on top of day-6 sensitivity loss; act on finger-sticks until the trace is steady and agrees.

Day-to-day practice. Most current sensors are factory calibrated; when they allow a finger-stick calibration, it should be entered only with a flat trend arrow and clean, dry fingers, because a sugary finger reads falsely high.
Check. 0.15 × 12 = 1.8 mmol/L, the whole gap.

bank.q: Compare an enzyme electrode, an ISFET and a nanomaterial FET as the basis of a portable urea meter. Judge which you would choose for a clinic and give reasons.
outline: Enzyme electrode: urease converts urea to ammonium, amperometric or potentiometric readout, cheap and proven
ISFET: label-free, small, but drift and reference electrode problems
Nanomaterial FET: high sensitivity, but Debye screening in high-salt samples and reproducibility issues
Criteria: detection limit, linear range in urine, drift, sterility, cost per test, calibration burden
Recommendation with a stated trade-off
Controls and calibration plan for the chosen device
answer: Need. A clinic urea meter for serum (normal about 2.5–7.8 mmol/L, up to 50 or more in kidney failure), simple to run, low cost per test, and stable day to day.

Enzyme electrode. Urease over an ammonium ion-selective electrode (potentiometric) or a pH electrode. Proven, cheap, tolerant of serum. Ideal slope 59.16 mV per decade: a reading 40.0 mV above a 1.0 mmol/L standard gives 1040.0/59.16 = 4.75 mmol/L. Drawbacks: the logarithmic response compresses high values, K⁺ and Na⁺ interfere with an ammonium membrane, and the enzyme needs cold storage.

ISFET (EnFET). Urease on a pH ISFET. Very small, batch-made, fast, suits arrays. Drawbacks: drift of the sensing layer, reference electrode stability, light and temperature sensitivity, and a signal of only millivolts (2.95 mV for 0.05 pH) that depends on the sample buffer capacity.

Nanomaterial FET. Graphene or nanowire channel with urease or a receptor. Very sensitive in low-salt buffer, but in serum the Debye length is about 0.8 nm, so the sample must be diluted about 100 times (Debye length 7.9 nm), and device-to-device reproducibility is still poor.

Judgement. For a clinic, the urease enzyme electrode: it measures undiluted serum over the whole clinical range, its behaviour and failure modes are well known, and two-point calibration each day is enough. The EnFET is the choice when many analytes must share one tiny chip; the nanomaterial FET is still a research device for this job.

Calibration and controls for the chosen device. Two standards bracketing the range (for example 2.5 and 25 mmol/L), checked every morning; a normal and a high control serum per batch; temperature at 37 °C or compensated; a slope below about 50 mV per decade flags a tired membrane.
Trade-off stated. The choice gives up miniaturisation for robustness and serum compatibility.

Running cost. An electrode with a replaceable urease membrane serves many tests, so the cost per test falls to that of the standards and controls; single-use FET chips must be made very cheaply to compete.

bank.q: Explain how Debye screening restricts label-free electrical detection of charged molecules, and analyse three ways to overcome it.
outline: Debye length about 0.7–0.8 nm in 150 mM salt; charge beyond it is screened from the electrode
Consequence: large targets and whole cells give weak signal in serum
Strategy: dilute the sample to lengthen Debye length
Strategy: move the binding event close to the surface, using short probes or fragmented targets
Strategy: use an optical or mass readout that ignores charge screening
State cost of each strategy: loss of sample realism or added steps
answer: What screening is. Ions in a salt solution crowd around any surface charge with opposite sign, so the electric field of a charge dies away over a short distance, the Debye length λD. A FET or electrode senses only charge inside this layer.
Size. For a 1:1 salt at 25 °C, λD ≈ 0.304/√I nm with I in mol/L.

Consequence. An IgG antibody is about 10–15 nm long. An antigen captured at its tips sits several nanometres from the gate, that is several Debye lengths away in serum, and its charge is almost fully screened. Large proteins, whole cells and long DNA give weak or no direct signal in undiluted samples.

Strategy 1: dilute or desalt. Diluting 100 times lengthens λD ten times, to 7.9 nm. Cost: the target is also diluted 100 times, so the detection limit worsens, and low ionic strength can change binding.

Strategy 2: bring binding closer. Use small receptors instead of whole antibodies: antibody fragments (Fab, about 5 nm), aptamers or short DNA probes, so the bound charge lies within a nanometre or two. Cost: new receptor chemistry and possibly lower affinity.

Strategy 3: change the readout. Use an optical (SPR, fluorescence, gold colour) or mass (quartz crystal) readout that does not depend on charge, or a polymer layer such as PEG that raises the effective screening length at the surface. Cost: more optics or added layers and steps.
Other options. High-frequency impedance readout, or a labelled sandwich that brings a charged or redox label to the surface; both add steps.
Judgement. Strategy 2 keeps the sample realistic and the device simple, so it is the usual first choice; dilution is the quickest laboratory fix.

Worked check of strategy 2. If a 5 nm Fab fragment replaces a 12 nm IgG, the bound antigen moves from about 12 nm to about 5 nm from the gate; in tenfold diluted serum (λD 2.5 nm) that is two Debye lengths instead of about five, so much more of its charge is felt.

bank.q: Judge labelled versus label-free DNA detection for a fever panel that must run without a thermocycler.
outline: Labelled route: redox tag, intercalator or fluorophore; higher signal, extra washing steps
Sandwich format for longer targets and extra specificity
Label-free route: impedance or FET; simpler chemistry, more sensitive to matrix
E-DNA stem-loop gives reagentless, reusable sensing but single-step kinetics
Throughput, cost per test in rupees, shelf life, need for controls
Verdict tied to the stated requirement of no thermocycler
answer: Requirement. Detect several fever pathogens (for example dengue, malaria, typhoid) from a blood sample without a thermocycler. Amplification must therefore be isothermal: LAMP at about 60–65 °C or RPA at about 37–42 °C, both run on a simple heater.

Labelled route. A redox tag (ferrocene, methylene blue), an intercalator or a fluorophore reports the duplex. Signal is large and specific; a sandwich with a capture probe and a labelled detector probe adds a second sequence check. Cost: extra reagents and wash steps, and labels with limited shelf life.

Label-free route. Impedance or FET readout of the duplex itself. Simpler chemistry and fewer steps, but the signal is small, it is sensitive to the sample matrix and non-specific adsorption, and FETs suffer Debye screening (0.8 nm in serum).
E-DNA stem-loop. Reagentless and reusable: binding opens the stem and the current falls. It is signal-off, so probe loss looks like a positive unless the current is normalised.

head: Criterion
Labelled (sandwich, redox)
Label-free (impedance)
rows: one electrode per pathogen, same label

answer: Amplification makes the difference. LAMP makes about 10⁹ copies in under an hour, so the target is far above the picomolar limit of either readout, and specificity rather than sensitivity decides. LAMP also makes non-specific products, which a sandwich with a second probe rejects better than a single label-free probe.
Controls. Each panel carries a blank, a positive control for each pathogen and a human-gene control that proves the sample was amplified.

Verdict. A labelled sandwich with a redox label after isothermal amplification: the second probe guards against false positives from LAMP by-products, and the strong signal suits a cheap reader. Label-free impedance is the fallback where cost per test in rupees must be lowest.
Reader. A small battery potentiostat reads each electrode by square-wave voltammetry in about a minute, and a heater block holds 63 °C for LAMP; neither needs the power or cost of a thermocycler.
Check. 230 ≈ 1.07 × 10⁹, so 10⁹ copies corresponds to about 30 doublings, which isothermal methods reach without thermal cycling.

glossary.def: The specific substance the biosensor is built to measure.
Sensor that holds the electrode at a fixed potential and measures the resulting current.
Sensor that measures voltage at almost zero current, usually with an ion-selective membrane.
Electrode of known, stable potential, usually Ag/AgCl, against which the sensing electrode is measured.
Electrode where the reaction of interest is driven and the current is measured.
Small redox molecule that shuttles electrons from an enzyme to the electrode, allowing a lower operating potential.
Enzyme sensor that measures the natural substrate or product, such as oxygen or hydrogen peroxide.
Enzyme sensor that uses a mediator or redox dye to transfer electrons instead of relying on oxygen.
Sensor in which the enzyme transfers electrons directly to the electrode without a mediator.
Amount of substrate converted per unit time under stated conditions, usually in units per milligram.
Measure of how tightly an antibody binds its antigen; tighter binding lowers the detection limit but slows release.
Format where a capture probe binds the target and a second labelled probe binds a different site on the same target.
Combination of temperature, salt and detergent in a wash that removes mismatched duplexes while keeping perfect matches.
Short single-stranded nucleic acid of known sequence fixed on the sensor surface.
Electroactive group such as ferrocene or methylene blue whose proximity to the electrode changes the measured current.
Technique that measures how the electrode–solution interface resists and stores charge over a range of frequencies.
Relation giving electrode potential as a function of ion activity, about 59 mV per decade at 25 °C for a one-electron change.
Thin film that lets one ion pass or binds it, producing a charge at the surface of an ISFET or electrode.
Reduction of the effect of a surface charge by ions in the surrounding solution.
Permselective polymer film that lets small molecules through while blocking anions such as ascorbate.
Mean absolute relative difference, the usual accuracy measure for a continuous glucose monitor.
Paper-based test where labelled particles move by capillary action and are captured on a test line.
Ability of an implanted sensor to stay in the body without harming tissue or being fouled by it.
Build-up of protein and cells on a sensor surface that blocks the analyte and reduces signal over time.
